newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Siemens phone unit sees sales growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Siemens phone unit sees sales growth.

text.p: The private communications systems group of electronics giant Siemens AG said on Wednesday it expected growth in the United States and Asia to lift 1996/97 sales 15 percent to 10 billion marks ($6.4 billion).

Increasing worldwide sales of mobile and cordless phones and corporate communications devices should spark a further rise to 15 billion marks by 2000, group president Dietrich Botsch told a news conference.
"We have clearly beaten our targets and have grown much faster than the market as a whole," he said.
Pretax profit, which totalled 503 million marks for the year ended September 30, should also rise, although Botsch declined to say if it would keep pace with sales increases.
"I won't make any profit forecasts," he said. "The cost of entering new markets, declining prices of our products, increasing competition -- they all affect profit."
Even though worldwide sales of telephones, fax machines and other end-customer equipment are rising steadily, maintaining profit levels will be a challenge, analysts who follow Siemens said.
"Siemens can compete. The question is what prices can they get in emerging markets and when they go up against other big companies," said Hans Peter Wodniok, a Credit Lyonnais analyst in Frankfurt.
Botsch said falling prices force the group to compensate for a one billion mark drop in sales each year.

To continue growth against that trend, the private communications systems group (PN) expected U.S. sales to rise to 2.5 billion by 2000 from last year's 1.3 billion marks. In Europe, the group forecast a rise to seven billion marks from 5.3 billion in 1995/96.
Asian sales are now well under one billion marks but would reach 1.3 billion marks by 2000, when international sales should make up 60 percent of revenue, up from 40 percent today, Botsch said.
Productivity improvements should also lower costs by around two billion marks over the next two to three years, he said.

Sales of cellular and cordless telephone sets grew 40 percent to 2.6 billion marks in 1995/96. New picture phones, dual mode phones for data and voice transmissions, should help lift sales in the division to five billion by 2000, Botsch said.
At the same time, sales of communications systems for corporate networks and call centres were expected to rise to seven billion marks from six billion in 1995/96.
The group was the third most profitable Siemens unit last year, generating a fifth of group profit.
In the first quarter of its fiscal year, orders for the private networks division were higher than expected.
The company expects a return on sales of between five and six percent in the next few years after 5.1 percent in 1995/96.
